title: What other states can learn from Alabama’s literacy gains https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/what-other-states-can-learn-alabamas-literacy-gains
author: Meredith Coffey and David Griffith
summary: Meredith Coffey and David Griffith introduce Fordham's report on Alabama's reading gains, written by journalist Liana Loewus, as part of the institute's interest in the Southern Surge. They frame the story carefully: the data are noisy and many reforms overlapped, but science-of-reading policies are the most notable common thread. They note that the science of reading is reasonably settled while the science of its implementation is not. Alabama adopted literacy coaching in the early 2000s, dropped it, then recommitted after watching Mississippi borrow and succeed with the model. The authors draw three takeaways from the report: leadership at the state agency level, a multifaceted implementation strategy, and a coaching corps with defined roles and steady funding. They close by acknowledging that this is expensive financially and politically, but so is failing to teach children to read.
points: Alabama's progress is presented as the product of decades of sustained effort, not a single reform, with coaching adopted, dropped and then revived after Mississippi's example.
Evidence-based reading instruction starts at the top, with a state agency that understands the science and shapes classroom practice.
Implementation needs a multifaceted strategy, pairing training with approved curricula, a pyramid of coaches, a third-grade reading guarantee and political staying power.
Coaching works only with defined roles, ample support and steady funding, since skilled coaches do not appear overnight and can disappear when priorities shift.
The authors keep humility visible, noting noisy data and that knowing the science is easier than implementing it across thousands of classrooms.
quotes: For the past decade, a handful of Southern states have been on an upward academic trajectory (though, as usual, the data are noisy). The most notable reforms associated with this positive trend center on the science of reading (though, as usual, a lot of other things were happening).

Still, the journey remains long from “embracing the science” at the policy level to teaching reading effectively in thousands of classrooms. And, while the science of reading is reasonably settled, the science of its implementation is considerably less so.

Alabama first adopted literacy coaching in the early 2000s and subsequently saw the needle move on student reading achievement. While Alabama didn’t stick with it, Mississippi took heed and borrowed from its coaching model.

Simply put, there are right and wrong ways to teach reading. And they look pretty similar in Huntsville and Mobile—and Boise and Scranton and Cincinnati. So, it’s vital that state leaders push districts, schools, and individual teachers in the right directions (and equally vital that those same leaders get the science right).

After all, it’s one thing to require K–3 teachers to complete science-of-reading trainings. But it’s another thing entirely to provide a short list of approved curricula, build a sturdy pyramid of dedicated reading coaches, adopt a third-grade reading guarantee that pushes adults to intervene when students struggle, and stay the course when those policies generate pushback.

Skilled reading coaches don’t appear overnight. And they won’t appear at all—and might disappear—if they aren’t properly trained and supported, if the requisite funding doesn’t materialize, or if competing priorities distract them from their primary mission.
No, it’s not cheap, financially or politically. But then again, neither is a systemic failure to teach students to read.
